item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.content:encoded:
In reply to Grant Shalks.

Hi Grant, Good question…

I’m confused by “Nature is not reducible to polar opposites”.
Surely if anything characterizes nature, polar opposites do: dark / light, hot cold, fertile/infertile etc.

First, let’s review: In The Principles of Quantum Mechanics (1930), Paul Dirac contrasted the traditional common sense Newtonian world and the quantum one: “It has become increasingly evident… that nature works on a different plan. Her fundamental laws do not govern the world as it appears in our mental picture in any direct way, but instead they control a substratum of which we cannot form a mental picture without introducing irrelevancies.”

Our words and language form much of this mental picture and thereby introduce irrelevancies. More precisely, the words and language we use to think about the world arise from the electro-chemical ON / OFF nature of the nervous system (neurons). This biology forces us to perceive reality in a dipolar way. While this ON/OFF process is just a speck of nature’s cosmic reality, this speck is the primary process life relies on to perceive and maneuver through the environment (i.e. survive).

In other words, survival rather than perceiving nature’s cosmic reality is the driving force of evolution. Obviously, our large brain fosters vast and subtle features of this ON/OFF process compared with protozoa or plants, for example. Alas, that advantage allows human language to exacerbate this dipolar perceptual bias.This link should retrieve some information on this dipolar situation. https://centertao.local/?s=dipolar

Chapter 1 addresses this language problem right off the bat…

The way possible to think, runs counter to the constant way.
The name possible to express runs counter to the constant name.

Chapter 70 offers a hint too…

Our words are very easy to know, very easy to do.
Under heaven none can know, none can do.
Speech has its faction, involvement has its sovereign.

Of course, our brains are wired for language, words, which depict nature in the only way words can, dipolar. When you loose your faith in the words you use to define the world you see, you become freer to see the world, nature, as it actually may be. Chapter 71 bluntly reveals this perceptual problem, and a way to manage it.

Realizing I don’t’ know is better; not knowing this knowing is disease.

I hope this helps a little. I’d just say, this Taoist thought journey takes a lifetime to travel and realizations trickle out over that time span. That’s a good thing. I mean that is one fine benefit of aging. The only one, I suppose. 🙂

carl

item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.description:
In reply to <a href="/2017/01/04/the-tradeoff/comment-page-1/#comment-1704173">Lynn Cornish</a>.
RE: "I don't get your thinking of hunter gatherers as being less clinging than we are." It is just that they don't have the opportunity to cling as much. Also, they cling to each other. Social clinging is a primal instinct for a social species. A hierarchical social system (civilization) isn't as conducive to social connection ('clinging') as the primal egalitarian social system of our ancestors. As a result, we seek out a vast array of other 'thing' (materials and stories) on which to cling. Alas, none of these substitutes are as meaningful (connecting) as the old way. In being raised in a hierarchical system, we are primed to notice the 'best'. Having the 'best' feeds into our hierarchical paradigm. Having the 'best' is not a big deal when you are born, live, and die in an egalitarian paradigm where life is much more a shared experience.
RE: "Also, animals sure do experience regret". Of course, all animals experience 'regret'. Need and fear are survival drives. Not getting what an animal feels it needs will evoke 'regret'. The impact of this upon civilized humans became more intense as we lost the deep social security that the 'old way' provided. Since the tradeoff, we are more insecure from the get-go (say age 2 onward?). I see Buddha's Truths a applying to all life on earth… up to a point. For more on this see, https://centertao.local/2016/05/30/truth-pertains-to-all-life/
RE: "P.S. you need more pets in your life." Done! I go to the beach to visit 'my' creatures everyday (and do my tai chi and yoga). Of course, my 'pets' are free to fend for themselves and feel no obligation to serve my needs. In fact, I regard them as my teachers too; they point the way to returning to authenticity.
As always, great questions Lynn!

item.title: By: Lynn Cornish
item.dc:creator: Lynn Cornish
item.description:
This is quite a treatise! Thank you Carl for putting it all together. You thinking is familiar to me, of course, because of our past correspondence. It’ll be familiar to you that I ask questions!
I don’t get your thinking of hunter gatherers as being less clinging than we are. I suppose it could be true, since they were wanderers and couldn’t take much stuff along, but weren’t they more like us and just clung to different things? The pointiest rock or best food or aspiring to a better hut or cave?
Also, animals sure do experience regret. You should see Willy after he gets in the garbage. One time, I’ll never forget, he was acting so guilty but we never discovered what he did. That was exceptional because his guilt was all in his head...he didn’t pick up signals from us because we didn’t know about it but he knew whatever he did, it was "bad." I wish I had a video of Bad Willy. I’m aware that my thinking about this might be wrong. He may have just been remembering the last time he did that particular wrong behavior and how he was punished. It may not have been regret at all. But still....he was reacting to his own thoughts. What do you think? P.S. you need more pets in your life.

item.title: By: Theresa Domenici
item.dc:creator: Theresa Domenici
item.description:
I understand it is the ongoing questioning that drives me. I am fortunate I remain curious. The question I am now pondering has to do with this practice of performing one's duty, and identifying ones so called "yoga". I practice physical yoga by being quiet and setting aside a time to give time on my yoga mat but I haven't deeply pondered what drives me to the practice day in and day out. It is one constant in my life and has been for very many years. My practice might've started as a physical /emotional health tool that more recently evolved to be a grounds for observing my own imbalance. Now i'm beginning to wonder : perhaps it is the sheer act of giving to something other than myself that I therefore feel more unified with myself and a more inclusive whole? By forgetting my self , by placing myself last, that I find my self in a more whole universe??
There is something about bowing down, surrendering, sacrificing to something outside of myself that seems to fill My void. For the most part, when I am practicing yoga, I am not expecting a huge outcome. I guess it could be said that it is faith that drives me to return to the yoga mat .... Or at the very least it is a willingness to give to a practice ..... A practice that does not ensure a particular outcome on any particular day
P S There are instances when "NOT getting on my yogamat" offers me a different opportunity to practice yoga. Times when I am derailed from practicing what I project to be helpful to me or more generally, derail me from my "agenda", can allow me to witness my own in balance in this particular pursuit.

item.title: By: Dian Duchin Reed
item.dc:creator: Dian Duchin Reed
item.description: This is a very clear, succinct summary of your views, which I have always appreciated. What I especially enjoyed here was your view on one's yoga--the importance of discovering what it is and carrying it out: "Any life pursuit that fulfills that duty [yoga, meaning “to join”, “to unite”] will work." Do you have any more writings on this subject?

item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.description:
I truly appreciate the dilemma you voice. We naturally live life in the present and so have trouble being outside our life “in the vast expanse”. How can we do as chapter 7 hints, <a href="https://centertao.local/tao-te-ching/carl/chapter-7/">The wise person places his life last yet life comes first, <b>Is outside his life, yet lives life</b></a>?
Whatever issue currently troubles us easily bogs us down by forcing us to “place our life first”. I find seeing the connection between what troubles me most and the all-pervasive hierarchical dynamics of civilization brings me significant closure, as they say. In effect, that helps me “place my life last”. I suppose it is the therapy of just knowing why, what, and how things are the way they are... Why it is what it is. That helps me “be outside my life, yet live life”.
To elaborate: I now always suspect ‘the civilization process’ to be responsible for whatever troubles me at <u>any given moment!</u> That initial suspicion stimulates me to seek the connections (cause and effect details) that support or refute my suspicion. I appreciate that there is an ongoing conflict between humanity’s innate egalitarian nature vis-à-vis the all-pervasive hierarchical dynamics of civilization. All I need do is fill in enough details to resolve each personally troubling particular situation. Finding those details, those connections, helps confirm for me emotionally “it is what it is”. This frees me to simply “Strive on diligently” as Buddha suggests.
Focusing on and resolving whatever disturbs me in this rational impartial way allows me to dig out completely the splinter irritating me now. Doing that diligently seems to bring closure and peace, until the next splinter comes along. Then I deal with it just like the last.
I hope that makes some sense, and not just more “vast expanse”. All that is necessary, I feel, is to appreciate the overall outline of how we ended up here — the “vast expanse of human evolution” — yet keep to the present and apply that ‘appreciation’ to the troublesome issue at hand, at any given moment. Keep one eye on the vast expanse and one eye on the solid ground of the moment-to-moment.

item.title: By: Theresa Domenici
item.dc:creator: Theresa Domenici
item.description: Again, I am always appreciative of the culmination of your observations particularly because they serve as a kind salve administered to my own criticisms of my inability to understand my place in civilization. Upon my first reading today, I come away perplexed by my own inability to get a feeling for how brief My time living here actually is and how far back it all stretches for human beings at least as you laid out in your essay. I'm gonna start paying attention to the emotional feeling I get for trying to place myself in The vast expanse of human evolution as you outlined. I always hear these numbers and timelines but I don't have enough feeling for it; I don't quite know where to place it emotionally in my life so that I can retrieve it and massage it and observe more of my understanding of those concepts, in action
